transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-25
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Redwood solutions), Priya Shah (Head of ML, Cedar Tech), Ethan Cole (Platform), Marta Novak (Security), Samir Rao (Infra)

Summary:
Quick discovery to understand Cedar Tech's latency and throughput SLAs for a customer-facing real-time assistant. Primary questions: p95 latency targets for streaming completions, concurrency (number of concurrent users and requests), token/sec benchmarking for their prompt mixes, and security requirements re: VPC/private deployment and KMS. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, benchmark plan, and next steps to run a pilot.

Topics: p95 latency, concurrency, streaming tail latency, token/sec benchmarks, dedicated capacity, VPC/KMS/SOC2, rollout timeline

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'm lena, i'm the AE on this. quick intros?
[00:08] Priya Shah: hi i'm priya, head of ml at cedar tech. excited to talk latency, we've got pretty tight p95 needs.
[00:12] Marco Ruiz: marco, redwood se, i'll dig into perf and benchmarks later.
[00:17] Ethan Cole: ethan, platform, i'll own infra questions and how this plugs into our stack.
[00:21] Marta Novak: marta from security, i have a few compliance items.
[00:25] Samir Rao: samir, infra ops.
[00:27] Lena Park: awesome. so high level, can you give us the use case and the p95 targets you're trying to hit?
[00:33] Priya Shah: sure. user-facing chat assistant, we stream tokens as they arrive. goal is p95 end-to-end of 250ms for short completions (like 20-40 tokens) and for longer completions we want p95 under 1s for each streaming chunk — basically low tail latency so UX feels instantaneous. concurrency is a big one — we expect spikes to 3k concurrent active sessions during launch, sustained 800 qps on average, peak short bursts to 5k qps during campaigns. token/sec wise our prompt mixes vary: approx 60% short prompts (30-50 tokens total), 30% medium (200-400 tokens), 10% long (1k+ tokens).
[01:10] Marco Ruiz: ok that's helpful. when you say p95 250ms is that time-to-first-token or end-to-first-chunk?
[01:16] Priya Shah: mostly time-to-first-token for the short ones. we care about first-byte because our UI displays typing immediately. tail latency for later tokens also matters but is slightly relaxed.
[01:25] Ethan Cole: and from infra perspective we run on multi-az in gcp, private VPC peering to partners, we need either dedicated capacity or private deployment for data controls and egress limits.
[01:35] Marta Novak: SOC2 type 2 is table stakes. also SSO/SAML, audit logs, encryption with customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) and no plaintext storage of user data.
[01:44] Lena Park: totally expected. Redwood has hosted, dedicated and private options — hosted is fastest to start; dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput; private (VPC or on-prem) gives you control for egress and KMS. we'll map these to your requirements.
[01:56] Marco Ruiz: on the perf side, streaming first byte latency is influenced by model, batch sizing, KV cache hits, and routing. we typically benchmark across model variants — e.g., 7b quantized, 14b, and a 70b variant — and produce token/sec and p95 curves for each under your traffic mix.
[02:10] Priya Shah: can you run quantized models in dedicated? we want to keep GPU costs down but maintain quality.
[02:15] Marco Ruiz: yes, dedicated supports quantized variants. and we recommend particular kernel paths depending on hardware. there's a tradeoff: heavy quantization saves cost but sometimes adds tail latency for long-context streaming, depends on attention kernels.
[02:28] Ethan Cole: two practical questions: how do we validate p95 under our concurrency pattern? do you run ramp tests? and what's the tooling?
[02:36] Marco Ruiz: we run token/sec microbenchmarks and distributed load tests that replay your traffic shape. we can run ramp & soak tests on dedicated pools. for hosted we can run isolated benchmarks but for strict guarantees dedicated SLA is better. we capture p50/p95/p99, throughput, and cost per 1k tokens.
[02:50] Priya Shah: if you run a hosted pilot with our prompts, does data get stored? we can't keep PII.
[02:56] Lena Park: hosted by default doesn't use your data for training; we have retention settings and enterprise offerings for private control plane. for full data isolation and customer-managed KMS you'd pick Private deployment or Dedicated with VPC and KMS integration.
[03:08] Marta Novak: need to see SOC2 docs and proof of KMS integration, also audit logs per request at token level if possible.
[03:14] Lena Park: we'll include SOC2 and KMS integration notes in the doc package.
[03:18] Marco Ruiz: back to perf — what hardware are you expecting? does Cedar want to use GPU type X (A100/p4d?) or cloud-managed instances?
[03:26] Ethan Cole: we're standardizing on GA4 and A100-equivalent in GCP, but open to dedicated supplier suggestions. price will matter.
[03:33] Marco Ruiz: ok. for A100-family we can typically get first-token p95 around 100-200ms for small models under low contention; under high concurrency with batching, first token can increase because of batching windows — but we have continuous batching heuristics to keep time-to-first-token low. dedicated gives you predictable concurrency so batching can be tuned.
[03:50] Priya Shah: what's your recommended batching policy for streaming? real-time typing needs small batch windows, right?
[03:55] Marco Ruiz: correct. we use adaptive batching: short window for low-latency routes, heavier batching for throughput routes. for your profile (mix of short and medium) we'd suggest separate routes: low-latency route with target tail p95 250ms and throughput route for background tasks.
[04:08] Samir Rao: do you support prefix/KV cache to speed repeat requests? we have many repeated user prompts.
[04:12] Marco Ruiz: yes, KV/prefix caching is supported and can drop per-token cost significantly. but cache hits need to be tuned; for streaming the initial token still has some compute.
[04:20] Priya Shah: about token/sec metrics — can you share how you measure tokens/sec? is it tokens per GPU sec or end-to-end tokens/sec at serving layer?
[04:27] Marco Ruiz: we report both: tokens/sec per-device (model throughput) and effective tokens/sec at the API layer accounting for concurrency and batching. we'll provide both in the spreadsheet.
[04:35] Ethan Cole: what's the plan for measuring p95 under 3k concurrent sessions? do you simulate sessions or open many persistent connections?
[04:41] Marco Ruiz: we simulate sessions and persistent streaming connections to match your browser long-poll style. we can replay user sessions with jitter and simulate cold/warm KV cache states.
[04:50] Priya Shah: for p95 targets, do you have historical numbers you can show for similar customers? like p95 for time to first token at 3k concurrency?
[04:58] Marco Ruiz: we have benchmark examples — typical numbers: with dedicated capacity on A100 equivalent, first-byte p95 ~220-350ms at multi-thousand concurrency depending on model size and batching. smaller models hit 120-220ms. I'll share the benchmark sheet with curves.
[05:12] Lena Park: note that streaming affects perceived latency; first-byte matters most. also consider model distillation or smaller specialized models for short-turn tasks.
[05:21] Priya Shah: have you observed tail spikes because of KV cache evictions?
[05:24] Marco Ruiz: yes if cache eviction policy is aggressive you'll see variance. we expose cache config, and for private deployments you can size memory to reduce evictions.
[05:32] Marta Novak: security: how do you handle encryption at rest and in transit, and do you support customer-managed keys in private?
[05:37] Lena Park: we support TLS in transit, encryption at rest; in Private and Dedicated we support customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations. hosted supports envelope encryption with our keys unless you opt for enterprise KMS.
[05:49] Marta Novak: audit logs per request matter — do you have logs that show per-request model version, route, and token usage?
[05:54] Marco Ruiz: yes we log request metadata, model version, route, tokens consumed; retention policies can be configured. for private we can give full access to logs.
[06:02] Ethan Cole: latency SLOs — do you offer SLA guarantees on p95?
[06:06] Lena Park: we offer availability SLAs; for latency SLOs we offer guidance and we'll guarantee throughput and uptime for Dedicated tiers, but latency SLAs are nuanced because they depend on customer traffic shape and model choices. we do contractual SLOs for enterprise Dedicated customers — we can discuss targets in the pilot.
[06:23] Priya Shah: okay, what's a realistic pilot? we'd like a 2-week pilot with our prompt set to measure p95 under our traffic, can you run that on dedicated?
[06:31] Marco Ruiz: yes, we can provision a small dedicated pool for a pilot. typical pilot flow: onboarding, deploy model variants, run baseline token/sec and p95 tests, then ramp to your concurrency pattern.
[06:41] Samir Rao: what sort of data ingress/egress setup will be needed for VPC peering?
[06:45] Lena Park: we'll share a network runbook: requirements for VPC peering, IP allowlists, NAT, and permissions.
[06:50] Priya Shah: any gotchas with streaming and WebSocket connections? we use server-sent events from the browser.
[06:55] Marco Ruiz: SSE or websockets both supported. persistent connections consume concurrency slots; we'll size capacity accordingly. with dedicated you control max concurrent streams per node.
[07:05] Ethan Cole: cost question: if we jump to dedicated to satisfy p95, how much more expensive vs hosted?
[07:09] Lena Park: generally dedicated has higher fixed cost but lower variability and better per-token economics at scale. hosted is variable usage-based; dedicated makes sense if you need predictable capacity and data isolation. we'll send concrete numbers.
[07:19] Priya Shah: regarding tokenization — do you charge on tokens in vs tokens out? we need clarity for billing.
[07:24] Lena Park: we bill on total tokens processed (consumed + generated). we'll include the billing model in the pricing doc.
[07:29] Marco Ruiz: to be explicit on benchmarks, we'll run three model profiles: small quantized (7b-q), medium (14b), and large (70b/opt). we'll provide p50/p95/p99 for time-to-first-token and per-token throughput curves for your prompt mix.
[07:43] Priya Shah: can you instrument client-side to capture perceived latency vs server metrics?
[07:47] Marco Ruiz: yes we have tracing hooks and you can add client timestamps; we also expose per-request trace ids to correlate front-end/ backend.
[07:54] Marta Novak: for compliance we need a runbook on data deletion and retention.
[07:58] Lena Park: will include retention controls and support for data deletion requests.
[08:02] Priya Shah: what about autoscaling behavior on dedicated? we want to avoid cold-start latency when scaling up for bursts.
[08:08] Marco Ruiz: dedicated supports capacity pools with warm nodes and burst capacity. autoscaling can be configured aggressively with warm pre-provisioning to avoid cold starts; there's also canary rollout.
[08:18] Samir Rao: if we go private on-prem, how involved is installation and does it change benchmarks?
[08:23] Marco Ruiz: on-prem gives you control over hardware and networking; benchmarks depend entirely on your hardware selection and network topology. we provide an ops package and run an onboarding benchmark.
[08:33] Priya Shah: ok let's talk acceptance criteria — what would success look like for the pilot?
[08:38] Ethan Cole: success = p95 time-to-first-token <= 300ms for short prompts at 3k concurrency; sustained throughput >= 800 qps; stable cost per 1k tokens within pilot budget. also SOC2 docs provided and KMS integration validated.
[08:52] Priya Shah: agreed. and we want streaming perceived latency under 350ms p95 for short interactions.
[08:59] Marco Ruiz: that is achievable with dedicated and the right model choices. we'll tailor the pilot config: small low-latency model route and medium route for longer completions.
[09:08] Lena Park: i'll follow up with pricing and a pilot proposal. we'll include a benchmark plan and ask for sample prompt set and traffic CSV from you.
[09:15] Priya Shah: we'll share a sample of 5k anonymized sessions and the traffic distribution. can you simulate real-world jitter and cold-warm cache states?
[09:21] Marco Ruiz: yes we'll include jitter, burst windows, cold-start percentages, and cache-eviction scenarios in the load tests.
[09:30] Marta Novak: last security note — we may need a Data Processing Addendum and a standard vendor security questionnaire filled out.
[09:36] Lena Park: we'll attach the DPA and a completed vendor security questionnaire template.
[09:40] Samir Rao: any blockers for us to start the pilot?
[09:43] Lena Park: the major things are access to sample prompts, traffic shape CSV, desired model size preference, and security checklist. once we have those we'll schedule the pilot provisioning.
[09:52] Priya Shah: timeline — can we do a pilot in early march?
[09:55] Lena Park: yes propose pilot start 2027-03-08.
[09:58] Marco Ruiz: i'll tentatively block time for benchmarking and set up a deliverable schedule.
[10:02] Priya Shah: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[10:05] Lena Park: thanks all — recap in notes and next steps in the follow-up email.

Recap / Close:
- Pilot: 2-week dedicated pilot to run p95 / token/sec benchmarks with Cedar prompt set, target start 2027-03-08.
- Deliverables: benchmark spreadsheet, pricing/SLA doc, SOC2 & KMS notes, network runbook, DPA and vendor security questionnaire.
- Owners: Lena (pricing + docs), Marco (benchmarks + test harness), Ethan (traffic samples), Marta (security Qs).
